title: Please destroy my game, thanks
author: Square-Yam-3772
selftext:
so I have been trying to push this concept out of the prototype/demo phase and I went through another revamp based on the previous round of feedbacks. 

* added a tutorial
* improved the creature visuals
* made the game less static
* tried to make the ult more dramatic
* adjusted the main mechanic so it is not as dominating 

I am currently trying to polish/improve the gameplay so I would really appreciate it if you can give the demo a try for a few minutes and see what works/doesn't work for you

tool used: Unity3d + Codex CLI + GPT/Gemini for graphics

playable web build (not mobile friendly): [https://chooon.itch.io/signal-pit-bullet-hell-beasts](https://chooon.itch.io/signal-pit-bullet-hell-beasts)

note: get the steam demo if you want gamepad support

to mods: I hope this is okay for making multiple posts for the same project

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
people on this sub seem to think the concept is cool but I am still stuck with the refinement phase

I initially was going to dive straight into adding the trainer npcs and character dialogs for a story mode but I have been told to tighten up the gameplay first

it is not going to be a long game so it would be nice if I can get to a point where people wouldn't mind spending 15-20mins on it (that would be a personal best since my other games haven't been getting that kind of play time either)

replies.author: peetorskeetor
replies.body: Power ups mid-battle? Ala hades where things synergize and such.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
hades has a great system but other feedback already helped me plan my next revamp:

\- it turns out power ups (even minor ones) needs to happen every few seconds

\- similarly, something needs to happen every few seconds i.e. small enemy getting blown up

\- I should just turn it into a twin stick shooter (someone pointed me to some classic/famous game as a baseline and that helps because it is also a small room type of game)

I got my plates full right now but hades is actually a good one I think.

replies.author: Uncl33
replies.body:
then for 15-20 minute experience I would create 5-10 quick and completely different versions of core gameplay. And see what sticks.  
You don't need more features, you need unique and quirky loop with just enough depth to catch attention. I think you won't get there with polishing the current direction.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
someone recommended a classic twin stick shooter as a baseline/inspiration and that kind of make sense. I am going to pivot to that first and see if it works out. 

I am keeping the visuals and the basic thesis the same but I am redoing the loop so that it is closer to the typical experience i.e. should have a lot of stuff happening on screen every few scenes, spatial pressure instead of just stats

I am not sure why it didn't dawn on me initially. Maybe I was focusing on the asset generation too much

replies.author: Uncl33
replies.body:
I would try to dive deep into monster theme. Right now the projectile gameplay is totally abstract and disconnected from the character presentation.   
I would expect brutal fights, flying limbs, dynamics animation etc.   
Is fighting game what you want to make?   
Is bullet hell?   
Ask yourself - how does the visuals work with the mechanics - both should strengthen the other in a feedback loop.

(I dont know if you played pokemon before but this is basically two staryu-like creatures shooting at each other)

I don't know if I want to go in the direction of "flying limbs" (that would move the rating up)

what kind dynamic animations do you think would help? I can brainstorm on that

good question... I think the visuals and the gameplay in this iteration are coexisting better than the last iteration but I am not sure about "strengthening each other"

replies.author: Achilleas90
replies.body:
Yes it is wrong. The best is. Start with shapes and make it fun. Then you can find theme and art when it works. Because many times it won’t work. And you just spent time on art that is not needed now.  
You will learn as you go as long as you don’t keep hitting your head on the wall. It’s good that you ask help and critique.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
I got introduced to the process of greyboxing a while ago but I still found that concept very foreign. 

I am still wrapping my head around that one. Maybe it is something like "the shapes should feel good to control and I got a winner if people dont mind playing with these shapes for 30min-1hour"

replies.author: Achilleas90
replies.body: Yes you got it. The reason you use shapes is also because it is super fast. You can imagine the graphics. But it has to feel good and be interesting first. And when you don’t see effects and art on top, you can more easily see what’s wrong and what needs improvement. The graphics are just the cherry on top. You can test and scrap in a session. And learn from it for the next one.

comments.author: VikingKingMoore
comments.body:
This looks pretty boring and basic, it’s just….dots hitting other dots as you’re trying to hit the enemy? This isn’t bad for a learning project, but it looks like other new dev ai games. Slow, Static, barely moving animations, slow movement, the 3 upgrades when you lvl up, mix of art styles like you cut up different magazines and glued it together with no care about style or cohesion, like old new grounds games. 

There are tons of fun 2d arena action rigs, you didn’t bother playing any to get a sense of quality? Take a break from your game, go play similar games that had success, understand the areas you can improve compared to those.

replies.author: Square-Yam-3772
replies.body:
someone recommended a game to me but it is a old japanese console game so I just stared at the gameplay video a bit to try to borrow from that game

Initially, I made it so that the monsters would take turn being the boss but that didn't work out too well (one person mentions that the monster being the boss would just win... which is true in the previous build)

I tried to push this project a bit further than a learning project because I was told that it is a fun concept but now it is back to "boring and basic". this experience kind of make me rethink the whole prototype-> demo -> game pipeline.

Play newer stuff in that general area you’re building for, devs spend years designing and scrapping before they release a success.

replies.author: VikingKingMoore
replies.body:
You have 1 mob you’re fighting against. And what’s with the spiral fireballs that go on all sides if the enemy is only on the right? Seems like a huge design flaw. I shoot out 20 blue balls in a circle, only 1/4 actually reaches the other side of the arena where the enemy is, and only 1 hits. I spend 3 minutes just moving awsd in a small confined area, with nothing to do other then pick super super boring choices that also sometimes are double edge swords.

Vamp slayer succeeds because you are also gaining new weapons, exploring the level, and managing your spacing. Then you are given lots of choices for upgrading your game. Even if the choices aren’t exciting, it feels impactful and its affects are your characters. You start progressing faster, feel more powerful, and that cycle keeps bringing people back. 

I think you can do way way better, but you have to get off that stubborn tree stump and study games that already have success and an audience that overlaps with yours. really pay attention to the designs at a deeper level. It’s not just the animations, it’s pace, it’s upgrades, it’s progression, etc. 

If you want a slower paced monster battle then maybe make a monster rancher type where you don’t control what they do, but instead have to train and build loyalty before the monster really follows your commands. Then you can introduce training, tournaments, splicing new monsters, etc. 

Right now it’s vampire slayer but in a small room with 1 enemy for 3 minutes with 1 attack and super underwhelming upgrades. 

Anyways I’m talking too much, good luck!

comments.author: Building-Old
comments.body:
\- None of the menus or UI look very cohesive. It looks like a cobbled together mix of styles from various games. I don't think this is the kind of thing you can fix without having an actual artist work on it. 

\- The background art in the FIGHT/VS menu looks like it's from a 3D game with physically based rendering, which makes the gameplay art look crappy by comparison. There is a general principal in art that if you put two styles of art right next to each other in time and/or space, you're inviting comparison. More specifically, there is a principal in video games: showing realistic visuals sets higher expectations, both for the rest of the visuals and for the gameplay.  
  
\- During gameplay, the background the UI, the characters, and the effects are all different art styles as well as massively different levels of pixelated. I've done a decent number of game jams and this is giving 'week-long game jam game where the artist and the programmer didn't coordinate very well and the artist had to go visit family two days before the jam ended.' 

\- LIVE FIGHT BET NOW on its own makes sense as visual decorum, but putting it top center and aligning it to the player view makes it look like diegetic UI for the player, rather than set dressing. In other words, it's distracting in a way that players probably won't be able to describe. The sign should be aligned to the wall, putting it at a downward angle, and maybe not dead center, since that's a little uncanny.

\- The crowd moving around, and the tv screens changing is nice in and of itself. They are the only visual components I see that add production value above game jam level.

\- The upgrade menu is another completely different style with a ton of dead space and it's weirdly aligned to the top 1/3 of the screen.

\- The upgrades don't have unique, colorful icons that can be quickly identified by players so they don't have to read text every time. The chevrons are both boring and functionless. 

\- Do the red arrows on the right side of the upgrade buttons do anything?

\- Usually "initiative" refers to advantage at the beginning of a fight, not whatever it means here. See D&D for how that game uses it to get a feel for it.

comments.author: Achilleas90
comments.body:
Hey, I am that guy that said he will play the game the next day. Well I did! Here are my thoughts:  
  
I think there’s definitely something interesting in the core gameplay loop. The fast/simple structure works well and I can see the foundation of a fun arcade-style experience here.

A few things stood out to me while playing:

* The art direction is mostly stylistically consistent, but there’s a very noticeable mismatch in asset quality. The player/enemies look very high resolution and polished while the large background looks extremely low-res, so the contrast feels a bit strange visually.
* The tutorial image at the start is well made, but it felt a bit overwhelming to immediately memorize all controls and mechanics before even playing. I think the onboarding would work better if some mechanics were introduced gradually during gameplay with small contextual reminders like “Press Q to use ability” etc.
* The UI feels very mobile-oriented even though this is currently a desktop game. Ironically I think the game could actually work quite well on mobile with some control adjustments.
* It took me a while to understand how the central upgrade/progression bar worked. I think this system needs stronger onboarding plus more visual/audio feedback (“juice”) so the player emotionally connects the mechanic to becoming stronger.
* Repeated clicking to shoot became tiring pretty quickly. Auto-shoot would probably make the game feel smoother and let the player focus more on movement and positioning.
* Combat feedback could be improved. Damage doesn’t feel very impactful right now and sometimes it feels like the player is “shooting peanuts” even when winning. More hit feedback, reactions, effects, sound, screen shake, etc. would help a lot.
* There are also a few polish issues like sprite flipping pivoting from the edge instead of the center, which makes movement feel slightly awkward visually.
* The mid-round upgrade choices were difficult to evaluate because they use terms/mechanics the player doesn’t fully understand yet. The upgrades also didn’t feel impactful enough to significantly change the run.

Overall though, I think the core gameplay idea is interesting and there’s potential here. Most of the issues I noticed feel more like onboarding/feedback/polish problems rather than fundamental design problems.

comments.author: ZAPcon_64
comments.body:
I think the concept here is actually really interesting. The idea of taking a SHMUP type game and turning it into a 1v1 fighter is honestly really unique, at least it's not something I've personally seen before.

The only notes I can give from watching the video is that it does look like it would be a tad boring after a while. I think you should lean really heavier into the bullet hell aspect of it, especially if it is a single player game. That is: maybe every opponent is the equivalent of a SHMUP final level boss, with a number of unique bullet patterns and attacks; maybe even a few that disperse enemy ads onto the map while they go off screen for a bit?

You could maybe even take some design inspiration from Cuphead boss fights. Cuphead seems to be inspired by those old Contra games but also seems to have some bullet hell elements to it when it comes to some of the bosses. Might be a good place to pickup some interesting mechanics or other ideas to interpolate into your overhead game.

EDIT: While typing I saw the link for the demo and tried it out (the updated version) and here are a couple of quick thoughts I had.

1. Player control felt a little more sluggish than I would have liked especially when there are lots of ads to dodge around. I don't think it needs a huge boost, just something that felt slightly too slow to me.  
2. Only getting to move across half of the arena feels far too limiting in my opinion. If it were possible to move around the entire arena, that would open up the playable space and feel much more freeing as well as offer some more dynamic combat and more tactile play style when it comes to dodging attacks and ads. Would also give you more room to randomly drop hazards, or even populate power ups on the ground that you have to race for, and maybe that is where your battle upgrades come from?   
3. As I suspected above, after a while the game does start to feel just a bit boring, or that the fight has been dragging on for a while. I think if you try demoing some of the above changes, that might actually alleviate that, otherwise, in its current state, I would maybe suggest lowering the enemy health a bit? Just a thought!

Overall I still think this is a really cool idea and hope you stick with it and keep improving it. Hopefully even some of that was slightly helpful in your journey!
